query: How is laser power density chosen to avoid heating and damage when measuring Raman spectra of 2D materials?

hits.heading_path: Signatures of spin-phonon coupling in hematite crystallites through dielectric and Raman spectroscopy
hits.text: Raman spectra are acquired by using HORIBA LabRAM equipped with a green (Nd-YAG) laser of wavelength 532 nm. Temperature-dependent Raman spectra are recorded with the help of a heating/cooling microstage from Linkam Scientific (Model THMS600). Using the Linkam microstage, the temperature is controlled with an accuracy of ± 0 . 2 ◦ C. The laser power density on the sample surface, which is in the form of a pellet, is estimated to be ∼ 300 kW / cm 2 . This is considering a spot size of ∼ 1 µ m, numerical aperture ∼ 0.6, and laser power at the spot ∼ 3 mW.

Raman measurements . All the Raman measurements were carried out in vacuum using an optical cryostat (Oxford Micorostat He2) at temperatures from 10 to 295 K. The 514.4-nm (2.41 eV) line of diode-pumped-solid-state (DPSS) laser was used as the excitation source. The laser power was kept below 100 μ W to avoid damaging the samples. The laser beam was focused onto the sample by a ×40 microscope objective lens (0.6 N.A.), and the scattered light was collected and collimated by the same objective. The scattered signal was dispersed by a JobinYvon Horiba iHR550 spectrometer (2400 grooves/mm) and detected with a liquidnitrogen-cooled back-illuminated charge-coupled-device (CCD) detector. Volume holographic fi lters (Ondax and Optigrate) were used to clean the laser lines and reject the Rayleigh-scattered light. For polarized Raman measurements, an achromatic half-wave plate was used to rotate the polarization of the incident linearly polarized laser beam. In addition, the analyzer angle was used to selectively pass scattered photons with parallel or cross polarizations. Another achromatic half-wave plate was placed in front of the entrance slit to keep the polarization direction of the signals entering the spectrometer constant with respect to the groove direction of the grating 47 . The Raman spectrum of the substrate (SiO2/Si) was measured from the same location without samples at each temperature and subtracted from the sample spectrum after normalization by the intensity of the 520 cm -1 silicon phonon peak. The temperature dependence of the Raman spectrum of a bulk NiPS3 crystal was measured separately in a macro-Raman system by using a closed-cycle He cryostat. The excitation laser was focused by a spherical lens ( f = 75 mm) to a spot of size ~50 μ m with a power of 2 mW.

Raman spectra (Horiba Scientific, iHR series), at multiple spots, were obtained from the MoS2 flakes on all the devices using a 785 nm laser line under ambient conditions. All the measurements were performed by mounting the devices on a hot plate (ambient conditions). The hot plate was adjusted to the desired temperature, and a sufficient wait time was allowed in order for the device to attain the desired temperature. The temperature of the MoS2 sample on the device was verified using a handheld Infrared thermometer (OMEGASCOPE OS53x-CF), before, during, and after each set of measurements in order to check the accuracy and the consistency of the temperature control. A Coherent Cube solid-state laser system (Model 1069417) with a wavelength λ = 640 nm and with a circular spot size of a 3 mm diameter was used to illuminate the samples. Given that our laser spot size is ∼ 3 mm in diameter with 1 / e 2 value = 1 mm (manufacturer provided specification), it is generally assumed that this diameter of the laser light will uniformly flood the device area( ∼ 204 µm 2 ) as well as the nearby electrode areas surrounding the 2D sample. This uniformity prevents thermal gradients across the photoconductive surface/electrode combination thereby minimizing the possibility of any photothermal effect, as also explained in other investigations [28]. It is our understanding that the laser powers used in our experiments will also render this effect negligible. For example, as indicated in Ref. [28] at an applied power of 1 µW / µm 2 temperature gradient of less than 0.1 K are expected. In our experiment, the maximum power utilized ∼ 0 . 001 µW / µm 2 , about two orders of magnitude less than that of reference [28]. Therefore, contributions from the photo-thermoelectric effect can be considered as negligible [29]. The current-voltage measurements were performed using a Keithley Source meter 2400 Series, automated through an in house developed code using LabView.

hits.heading_path: 3.2. Raman spectra of layered MnPS3 at room temperature
hits.text:
Figure  2(a)  shows  the  Raman  spectra  of  MnPS3  samples  from  1L  to  8L  and  bulk, measured with the 488-nm laser line as the excitation source in the parallel polarization configuration [ ( ) z z xx ]. Whereas six Raman modes, P1 through P6, are observed from the bulk sample, the weak peaks P1 at ~120 cm -1  and P3 at ~230 cm -1 were not resolved in the spectra from few-layer MnPS3. The intensities of all the Raman modes gradually decrease as the layer number decreases as shown in Fig. 2 (b). Although the sample was kept in vacuum  at  all times, we  noticed that  some  degradation  occurred  during  Raman measurements even with the low excitation laser power of ~50 μW if the laser illuminates the same spot for an extended period of 500 s or longer (See Fig. S1 for details). In order to avoid such degradation, we obtained Raman spectra from multiple points within an area of ~10×8

μm [2]  with a short integration time (50 or 100 s) at each point and used the average of such spectra for better signal-to-noise ratios. The AFM topography image and Raman mapping show that the sample is highly uniform over the measured area. (See Fig. S2 and Fig. S3).
